    Iranian Officials Allowed To Enter US for UNGA

Alan Armstrong (R-OK) says the current energy crunch is exposing the cost of constrained infrastructure and strengthening the case for permitting reform. Bharat Ramamurti, Former Deputy Director of the National Economic Council, says President Donald Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend checks would be “unequivocally inflationary” and could force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further. (Source: Bloomberg)
    Ramamurti Says Rising Oil and Rates Risk Stagflation
    Bharat Ramamurti, Former Deputy Director of the National Economic Council, says President Donald Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend checks would be “unequivocally inflationary” and could force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further. Ramamurti says that continued rate hikes could push unemployment higher and that, if oil prices keep rising at the same time, the US risks ending up with stagflation alongside a weakening labor market. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Bloomberg Businessweek Daily: OpenAI Safety Incidents (Podcast)
    OpenAI shared several undisclosed incidents of its AI models misbehaving and unveiled a new framework for tracking and disclosing such occurrences going forward. Some of the previously unreported instances included OpenAI’s technologies concealing and fabricating information in order to return results, the company said in a blog post Wednesday. The ChatGPT maker has faced increased scrutiny since saying in July that some of its most advanced AI models had breached the systems of an external software company, Hugging Face. None of the newly disclosed misalignment incidents involved a hack or breach of a third party, OpenAI said in a separate statement. (Source: Bloomberg)
    Sen. Armstrong Says Energy Crunch Shows Infrastructure Gaps
    Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-OK) says the current energy crunch is exposing the cost of constrained infrastructure and strengthening the case for permitting reform. Sen. Armstrong points to the sharp gap in diesel prices between Oklahoma and California and the attack on Saudi pipeline infrastructure as examples of how limited capacity can leave consumers more vulnerable to price shocks. Sen. Armstrong says he is encouraged Congress could still act on permitting reform before the end of the session. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    AI Doom Drags On, Stocks Rebound
    OpenAI shared several undisclosed incidents of its AI models misbehaving, further fueling public concerns about the speed of growth of AI. Bloomberg News AI Reporter Shirin Ghaffary explains what OpenAI and others are doing to try and ease those fears. Plus, markets saw a rebound Thursday after falling the day prior on the heels of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates. Principal Asset Management's Chief Global Strategist Seema Shah discusses what's happening in the bon market. Then, Citi Head of Global Government Affairs Candi Wolff previews next week's meeting between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping. Finally, Bloomberg Intelligence US Homebuilding Analyst Drew Reading discusses the rising mortgage rates and the impact on homebuilder sentiment. All on the latest episode of "Bloomberg Businessweek Daily." (Source: Bloomberg)

    Trump himself has acknowledged the US need for Canadian aluminum – and has largely exempted metals from new tariffs As trade talks with Canada shambled toward collapse in late August, Donald Trump brayed on Truth Social: “WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” But in fact, Canada, like China, has something the US needs badly: critical metals that undergird modern military technology. Canada is the United States’s biggest foreign source of minerals, supplying about $47bin worth each year. Sixty per cent of all the aluminum the US uses each year, for instance, comes from Canada, where mighty, remote rivers provide smelting plants vast quantities of cheap, low-carbon electricity.     Trump’s love of fossil fuels is about more than money | Moira Donegan
    The US decision to remove limits on coal and gas plant emissions is rooted in a perception of manliness in these industries You can impress a certain kind of person at a party by reciting the fact that there are more yoga instructors in the US than there are coalminers. In fact, the disparity is greater than this catchy phrasing suggests: there are actually more yoga instructors in the US than there are people employed in the entirety of the coalmining industry, miners and otherwise. It’s not even especially close: about 38,000 people in the US work in coal, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, compared to about 100,000 yoga instructors who are registered with the Yoga Alliance, an industry group. If you looked only at the numbers, you might think a politician would be incentivized to talk about the interests of the yoga industry, about the dignity that yoga jobs give to American families, or about the need to foster growth in the yoga industry, more than they talk about these things for coal; after all, yoga, not coal, is putting food on the table in more American households. But no politician would ever talk about the interests of yoga teachers, or wax poetic about their role in the American dream, the way they do with coal miners; if they did, they’d be laughed out of the room. And we all know why: yoga is thought of as decadent, cosmopolitan and feminine, while coal mining is imagined as hardscrabble, honorable and masculine.     PlayStation 5; Insomniac Games Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore It was always going to be difficult to follow Spider-Man. Insomniac’s three games based around the web-slinger are masterpieces of superhero wish fulfilment, allowing you to swoop above a depiction of Manhattan alive with graffiti artists, roving journalists and gun-toting gangsters. If anyone should be up to the task, it’s Wolverine. A beloved Marvel stalwart, his life much darker and bloodier than Peter Parker’s, he seems the ideal protagonist for a moody action adventure. Yet somehow this well-made game falls short of its potential. Set years before the founding of the X-Men, Marvel’s Wolverine sees a disenfranchised Logan falling back in with Sabretooth and Mystique when their mentor Nathaniel Essex is kidnapped by mutant-hating billionaire Bolivar Trask. This archetypal tech bro has a disturbing plan for world domination and the X Team are out to stop him – but there is a secret buried in Wolverine’s past that’s about to cause an eruption.     Streaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened?
    Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is an ancient video of that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future. Since then, plenty of companies have tried to be the first to truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later. Continue reading...  ( 19 min )
